stem: Galactose and glucose are monosaccharides that both have the molecular formula C6H12O6, but one hydroxyl group is oriented differently, so the two molecules have different three-dimensional shapes. A permease in the plasma membrane of yeast cells imports galactose far more slowly than it imports glucose. Which statement best explains why the permease can distinguish between the two sugars?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The sugars contain different elements, so the permease binds glucose because it carries more atoms of carbon than galactose does.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The sugars contain the same atoms in different arrangements, so their shapes differ and only glucose fits the binding site of the permease well.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Galactose is a lipid with a hydrophobic backbone, so the permease cannot move it through the membrane as quickly as glucose.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The sugars are joined by different types of covalent bonds, so the permease recognizes the sugar that has the stronger bonds.

rationales.A: Both sugars are C6H12O6, so they contain exactly the same numbers of every element; the proposed difference in atoms does not exist.
rationales.B: The same atoms arranged differently give each sugar a distinct three-dimensional shape, and a transport protein binds the shape that fits its binding site.
rationales.C: Galactose is a carbohydrate, not a lipid; it has many hydroxyl groups and is polar, so its identity as a monosaccharide matches glucose.
rationales.D: Each sugar is a single monosaccharide; there are no bonds joining separate subunits, so bond type between monomers cannot explain the difference.

stem: Two tripeptides are made from the same three amino acids, alanine, glycine, and serine, but in the order Ala-Gly-Ser in one and Ser-Gly-Ala in the other. An antibody binds the first peptide strongly and the second one very weakly. Which statement best explains why the antibody can tell the two peptides apart?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The peptides have different total masses because order changes atoms, so the antibody binds the peptide with the greater mass.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The peptides have the same composition but different sequences, so the groups are arranged differently in space and fit the antibody differently.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The peptides contain different amino acids, so the antibody binds the peptide that has the larger number of different R groups.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The peptides use different kinds of covalent linkages between subunits, so the antibody binds the one with peptide bonds.

rationales.A: Rearranging the order of the same amino acids does not change the number or kind of atoms, so the masses are equal.
rationales.B: Sequence order changes which R groups sit where, giving a different three-dimensional shape and surface for antibody binding.
rationales.C: Both peptides contain exactly the same three amino acids; only the order differs.
rationales.D: Both peptides are linked by peptide bonds; the linkage type is identical.

stem: A mutation in a bacterial enzyme replaces a serine (polar, uncharged) on the protein's surface with leucine (nonpolar, hydrophobic). The mutant enzyme folds normally and remains active, but in water its molecules clump together into large aggregates, whereas the normal enzyme stays dispersed. Which best explains why the mutant molecules aggregate?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The leucine side chains form peptide bonds with neighboring enzyme molecules, joining the proteins into one large covalent polymer.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The exposed nonpolar leucine side chains on separate molecules associate with each other to avoid water, linking the molecules through hydrophobic interactions.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The leucine side chains form strong hydrogen bonds with water, which pulls the molecules together into aggregates.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The leucine substitution adds a negative charge, so the neighboring molecules are attracted to each other by ionic bonds.

rationales.A: Peptide bonds form only between the amino group and carboxyl group of amino acids during translation; R groups do not form them with other proteins.
rationales.B: Hydrophobic side chains exposed on the surface cluster together away from water, so separate protein molecules stick together.
rationales.C: Nonpolar side chains cannot form hydrogen bonds with water; serine, the polar residue that was replaced, could.
rationales.D: Leucine's side chain is nonpolar and uncharged, so it contributes no charge and no ionic attraction.

stem: Two subunits of a dimeric enzyme normally associate at an interface where aspartate 40 (negatively charged) on subunit A sits next to lysine 112 (positively charged) on subunit B. A mutation replaces lysine 112 with glutamate (negatively charged). The mutant subunits fold correctly but no longer form stable dimers. Which best explains the loss of dimer formation?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The attraction between opposite charges is lost and the two negatively charged side chains now repel each other at the interface.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The mutation breaks the peptide bond at position 112, so the subunit is cut in two and cannot reach the interface.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Glutamate is nonpolar, so it moves into the core of the subunit and no longer faces the interface where it could bind.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The glutamate side chain forms a disulfide bond with aspartate 40, which locks the surface of subunit B in the wrong shape.

rationales.A: Replacing the positive lysine with negative glutamate removes the ionic attraction and creates electrostatic repulsion.
rationales.B: The substitution changes an R group only; the peptide bonds of the backbone remain intact and the subunit folds correctly.
rationales.C: Glutamate has a charged carboxyl side chain and is polar; it would not be buried like a nonpolar residue.
rationales.D: Glutamate and aspartate contain no sulfur, so neither can take part in a disulfide bond; disulfide bonds require cysteines.

stem: In a small globular enzyme, valine at position 73 is normally buried in the interior of the folded protein, surrounded by other nonpolar side chains. A mutation replaces valine 73 with aspartate, which has a negatively charged side chain. The mutant protein folds poorly and loses most of its activity at body temperature. Which best explains this effect?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The negative charge of aspartate forms hydrogen bonds that are stronger than hydrophobic interactions and so improve stability.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Aspartate cannot form peptide bonds, so the polypeptide chain is cut at position 73 and the enzyme is shorter than normal.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A charged side chain placed in the nonpolar interior cannot interact favorably with the surrounding nonpolar groups, destabilizing the folded tertiary structure.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The aspartate substitution changes the primary structure only, and primary structure has no effect on folding of the polypeptide.

rationales.A: A mismatch of a charged group in a nonpolar core lowers stability; the mutant is less stable, not more.
rationales.B: Aspartate has the same amino and carboxyl groups as other amino acids and forms peptide bonds normally.
rationales.C: Charged groups are unstable in a hydrophobic core, so the protein's tertiary structure is disrupted.
rationales.D: The sequence of amino acids determines how the chain folds; changing one residue can alter tertiary structure.

stem: Two cells from a pond sample are examined by electron microscopy. Cell 1 is about 1 μm long, has a circular chromosome in a nucleoid region, 70S ribosomes, a flagellum, and no membrane-bound organelles. Cell 2 is about 15 μm long, has a nucleus, 80S ribosomes, chloroplasts, mitochondria, and a cellulose cell wall. Which conclusion is most directly supported by the observations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both cells are prokaryotic because both are single cells living in the same pond and cannot be classified by structure.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cell 1 is eukaryotic because it has a flagellum, which is a structure found only in cells that contain membrane-bound organelles.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cell 1 is prokaryotic because it lacks a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles, and Cell 2 is eukaryotic because it has both.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cell 2 is prokaryotic because it has a cell wall, and a cell wall is a feature that only prokaryotes possess.

rationales.A: Cells can be classified by structural features such as a nucleus, organelles, and ribosome type; habitat does not determine the cell type.
rationales.B: Prokaryotes can have flagella; a flagellum does not indicate eukaryotic classification.
rationales.C: Absence of a nucleus and of membrane-bound organelles marks a prokaryote (ribosomes are not membrane-bound organelles), and presence of a nucleus and membrane-bound organelles marks a eukaryote.
rationales.D: Plants, fungi, and algae are eukaryotes with cell walls, so a wall does not indicate prokaryote status.

stem: A researcher compares two cells. Cell 1 is about 100 μm in diameter, has circular DNA free in the cytoplasm, 70S ribosomes, and no nucleus or other membrane-bound organelles. Cell 2 is about 8 μm in diameter, has a nucleus, mitochondria, 80S ribosomes, and a chitin cell wall. Which conclusion about the cells is most directly supported by the observations?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Both cells are prokaryotic because both have ribosomes and DNA, which are the only structures all cells need.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cell 1 is eukaryotic because its larger diameter shows that it must contain a nucleus and organelles to support its size.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cell 2 is prokaryotic because its small size and its cell wall are characteristics found only in prokaryotic cells.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cell 1 is prokaryotic and Cell 2 is eukaryotic, because internal structure and not cell size separates the two types.

rationales.A: Ribosomes and DNA occur in both types; the nucleus, organelles, and 80S ribosomes show Cell 2 is eukaryotic.
rationales.B: Size does not determine classification; Cell 1 lacks a nucleus and organelles, so it is prokaryotic.
rationales.C: Cell 2 has a nucleus and mitochondria, which define it as eukaryotic; small size and cell walls occur in both types.
rationales.D: Absence of a nucleus and organelles defines Cell 1 as prokaryotic despite its large size; Cell 2 has a nucleus and organelles.

stem: A student weighs a potato core, places it in 0.6 M sucrose for one hour, and reweighs it. The core's mass falls from 5.0 g to 4.3 g, a change of -14%, and the tissue feels limp. A core placed in distilled water instead gains mass and feels firm. Which best explains the limp tissue in 0.6 M sucrose?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Sucrose entered the cells through the cell wall and replaced the cytoplasm, so the cells lost mass through exchange of sugar.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Water left the cells by osmosis because the sucrose solution was hypertonic, so turgor pressure fell and the tissue became limp.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The cells stopped using osmosis in sucrose, so the tissue lost mass through evaporation rather than through water movement.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Water entered the cells until the cell wall burst, which released fluid into the solution and lowered the mass.

rationales.A: Sucrose is a large solute that does not freely cross the membrane; the mass loss reflects water leaving the cells.
rationales.B: Net water moved out down its gradient, cytoplasm lost volume, and the loss of turgor made the tissue limp.
rationales.C: The measured loss arises from net osmosis out of the cells; sucrose does not switch osmosis off.
rationales.D: Water left the cells in the hypertonic solution; water entry produces firm tissue, not bursting.

stem: Plant biologists treat leaf cells with enzymes that digest the cellulose cell wall, producing protoplasts. Intact leaf cells placed in distilled water become firm but stay intact, whereas protoplasts placed in distilled water swell and many burst. Which best explains the difference in outcome?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Protoplasts lose their plasma membranes during digestion, so distilled water flows freely through them until they rupture.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Intact cells stay whole because their cytoplasm is isotonic to distilled water, whereas the protoplasts become hypotonic to it.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Without a wall, protoplasts have nothing to resist water entering by osmosis, so no turgor pressure limits swelling and the membrane ruptures.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The enzyme treatment makes the cytoplasm of protoplasts hypertonic to the intact cells, so water moves out until they burst.

rationales.A: The enzymes digest the cellulose wall, not the plasma membrane, which still bounds the protoplast.
rationales.B: Distilled water is hypotonic to both intact cells and protoplasts; the wall, not an isotonic cytoplasm, prevents bursting.
rationales.C: The wall provides counter-pressure that limits swelling in intact cells; removing it lets water entry continue until the membrane lyses.
rationales.D: Water moving out would shrink the cells; bursting results from net water entry in a hypotonic solution.

stem: A gardener waters houseplants with a very salty solution. Within hours the leaves droop, and under a microscope the plasma membranes of the leaf cells have pulled away from the cell walls. Plants watered with fresh water stay upright and firm. Which best explains why the plants watered with salty solution droop?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Salt entered the cells and made the cell walls swell, which pushed the plasma membranes away from the cell walls.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The cell walls dissolved in the salty solution, so the cells could no longer hold any water and the leaves drooped.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Water moved out of the cells by osmosis into the salty surroundings, so the cells lost turgor pressure and the tissue wilted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Water moved into the cells until the walls cracked, so the cells became flaccid and the leaves drooped.

rationales.A: The membrane pulls away because the cytoplasm shrinks as water leaves; salt does not swell the cell wall.
rationales.B: Cell walls do not dissolve in salt solution; the cells droop because of osmotic loss of water.
rationales.C: The salty solution is hypertonic to the cells, water leaves, turgor pressure falls, and the membrane pulls from the wall.
rationales.D: Water entry would raise turgor and firmness; drooping accompanies water loss.

stem: Developing red blood cells take up iron by receptor-mediated endocytosis. Iron-carrying transferrin in the blood binds to transferrin receptors in the plasma membrane, the membrane folds inward, and a vesicle carries the transferrin into the cell. A patient has a mutation that removes functional transferrin receptors from the cell surface. Which prediction is best supported by the described process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The cells will make extra receptors inside vesicles, which will move iron into the cytoplasm without any need for binding.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The cells will take in transferrin normally through the lipid bilayer, because diffusion of large proteins does not need membrane proteins.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Iron-loaded transferrin will remain in the blood while developing red blood cells receive too little iron, because transferrin cannot bind and be taken in.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Transferrin will be engulfed and then trapped in vesicles because the vesicles cannot move to the interior of the cell.

rationales.A: Nothing in the description allows iron to enter without receptor-mediated uptake; vesicles form after binding at the surface.
rationales.B: Transferrin is a large protein that cannot diffuse across the bilayer; its uptake depends on receptor binding.
rationales.C: Without receptors the transferrin cannot be recognized or engulfed, so it stays in circulation and the cells lack iron.
rationales.D: Without receptors transferrin is not engulfed, so no vesicles containing it form.

stem: Pancreatic beta cells store insulin in secretory vesicles. When blood glucose rises, the vesicles move to the plasma membrane, fuse with it, and release insulin outside the cell by exocytosis. A toxin prevents secretory vesicles from fusing with the plasma membrane but does not affect insulin synthesis. Which prediction is best supported by the described process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Insulin will be taken up into the cells by endocytosis, which lowers the amount of insulin in the vesicles.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Insulin will build up inside undelivered vesicles, and blood glucose will stay high because little insulin is released from the cells.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Insulin will diffuse through the phospholipid bilayer instead, so blood glucose will fall at the normal rate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Beta cells will stop making insulin completely, because the toxin blocks translation on ribosomes of the rough ER.

rationales.A: Endocytosis moves material into the cell; the toxin affects exocytosis, and import would not reduce stored insulin.
rationales.B: Fusion is required to release insulin, so insulin accumulates in vesicles and glucose remains elevated.
rationales.C: Insulin is a protein too large and polar to diffuse across the bilayer, so release depends on exocytosis.
rationales.D: The toxin affects vesicle fusion, and insulin synthesis is described as unaffected.

stem: Liver cells remove LDL from the blood by receptor-mediated endocytosis. LDL binds to receptors in the plasma membrane, the membrane folds inward, and a vesicle pinches off to carry LDL into the cell. A drug allows LDL to bind to the receptors normally but prevents the membrane from folding inward and pinching off. Which prediction is best supported by the described process?

choices.label: A
choices.text: LDL will pass through the membrane by diffusion because it is blocked from entering the cell by endocytosis.

choices.label: B
choices.text: LDL will not bind to receptors, because the drug stops the folding that makes the receptors able to bind LDL.

choices.label: C
choices.text: LDL will remain bound to receptors at the cell surface and not enter the cells, so blood LDL will rise.

choices.label: D
choices.text: LDL will be taken into vesicles faster than normal, because binding without pinching off concentrates it near the receptors.

rationales.A: LDL particles are large and cannot cross the bilayer by diffusion, so blocked endocytosis leaves them outside.
rationales.B: The drug is described as letting binding occur normally; binding happens before the membrane folds.
rationales.C: Binding is intact but the inward folding is blocked, so LDL is not internalized and is not cleared from the blood.
rationales.D: Without pinching off, vesicles cannot form, so uptake cannot speed up.

stem: Animal cells without a cell wall, whose cytoplasm has an osmolarity of about 280 mOsm/L, were placed in three unlabeled solutions for 10 minutes. In Solution P, the cells kept their normal shape. In Solution Q, the cells shrank and their surfaces became wrinkled. In Solution R, the cells swelled and about half burst. Which set of osmolarities is most consistent with the outcomes for P, Q, and R respectively?

choices.label: A
choices.text: P = 600 mOsm/L; Q = 280 mOsm/L; R = 50 mOsm/L

choices.label: B
choices.text: P = 50 mOsm/L; Q = 280 mOsm/L; R = 600 mOsm/L

choices.label: C
choices.text: P = 280 mOsm/L; Q = 600 mOsm/L; R = 50 mOsm/L

choices.label: D
choices.text: P = 280 mOsm/L; Q = 50 mOsm/L; R = 600 mOsm/L

rationales.A: At 600 mOsm/L the cells would shrink, not stay normal, and at 280 mOsm/L, which is isotonic, they would not shrink.
rationales.B: At 50 mOsm/L the cells would swell and lyse, not remain normal, and 600 mOsm/L would shrink them rather than burst them.
rationales.C: P is isotonic so no net water movement; Q is hypertonic so water leaves and the cells shrink; R is hypotonic so water enters and cells swell and lyse.
rationales.D: Q and R are reversed: a 50 mOsm/L solution is hypotonic and would cause swelling, while 600 mOsm/L would cause shrinking.

stem: Cultured animal cells with no cell wall have a cytoplasmic osmolarity of 300 mOsm/L. The cells are placed in three solutions that contain only solutes unable to cross the plasma membrane: Solution A at 150 mOsm/L, Solution B at 300 mOsm/L, and Solution C at 450 mOsm/L. Which set of outcomes is most likely for the cells in A, B, and C respectively?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A: cells swell and may lyse; B: no net change in volume; C: cells lose water and shrink

choices.label: B
choices.text: A: cells lose water and shrink; B: no net change in volume; C: cells swell and may lyse

choices.label: C
choices.text: A: no net change in volume; B: cells swell and may lyse; C: cells lose water and shrink

choices.label: D
choices.text: A: cells swell and may lyse; B: cells lose water and shrink; C: no net change in volume

rationales.A: A is hypotonic so water enters, B is isotonic so there is no net water movement, and C is hypertonic so water leaves.
rationales.B: The outcomes for A and C are swapped: 150 mOsm/L is hypotonic and causes swelling, while 450 mOsm/L is hypertonic and causes shrinking.
rationales.C: B matches the cytoplasm, so it is isotonic and would cause no net change; A is hypotonic and would not leave the cells unchanged.
rationales.D: B is isotonic and C is hypertonic, so the cells would not shrink in B or stay unchanged in C.

stem: Identical wall-less animal cells were placed in four solutions of non-penetrating solutes for 10 minutes, and the change in cell volume was recorded: Solution 1, +25%; Solution 2, -18%; Solution 3, 0%; Solution 4, -30%. Which ordering of the solutions from lowest to highest osmolarity is most consistent with the data?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Solution 4, Solution 2, Solution 3, Solution 1

choices.label: B
choices.text: Solution 1, Solution 2, Solution 3, Solution 4

choices.label: C
choices.text: Solution 3, Solution 2, Solution 1, Solution 4

choices.label: D
choices.text: Solution 1, Solution 3, Solution 2, Solution 4

rationales.A: This is the reverse order; the solution that caused the greatest swelling has the lowest osmolarity, not the highest.
rationales.B: This follows the order of the numbers in the list rather than the data; Solution 2 shrank cells, so it exceeds Solution 3.
rationales.C: This ranks by size of volume change, ignoring that swelling and shrinking occur on opposite sides of isotonic.
rationales.D: The more cells swell, the lower the solution's osmolarity; 0% change marks the isotonic point, and larger shrinkage means higher osmolarity.

stem: Plasma cells secrete antibodies. Antibodies are made by ribosomes on the rough ER, transferred to the Golgi complex for modification, and carried in vesicles from the Golgi complex to the plasma membrane for secretion. A drug blocks the fusion of those Golgi vesicles with the plasma membrane. Which outcome for antibody is most likely in the treated cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Antibody is released from the rough ER directly to the outside of the cell, bypassing the blocked Golgi vesicles.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Antibody is no longer made, because ribosomes on the rough ER stop translating when vesicles cannot fuse with the membrane.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Antibody is still made and enters the Golgi complex and vesicles, but it accumulates inside the cell and little is secreted.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Antibody is made by ribosomes in the vesicles instead, and the cells secrete it by a different route.

rationales.A: Antibody is not secreted straight from the rough ER; it must be processed in the Golgi complex and carried in vesicles.
rationales.B: The drug acts on vesicle fusion at the end of the pathway; it does not stop ribosomes from making the protein.
rationales.C: Synthesis and processing are intact; blocked fusion leaves the antibody in vesicles and little is released.
rationales.D: Ribosomes on the rough ER, not those in transport vesicles, make the antibody, and no alternative route is described.

stem: Hydrolytic enzymes that digest worn-out cell components are made by ribosomes on the rough ER, then modified and sorted in the Golgi complex into vesicles that become lysosomes. A drug prevents the Golgi complex from packaging these enzymes into vesicles but does not affect enzyme synthesis. Which outcome is most likely in the treated cells?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The enzymes are no longer made, because the Golgi complex supplies the ribosomes that carry out their synthesis.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The enzymes are digested by the Golgi complex, so worn-out components are broken down faster than in untreated cells.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The enzymes are made inside the lysosomes instead, so worn-out components are digested at the normal rate.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The enzymes are still made, but they do not reach lysosomes, so worn-out cell components are digested less and accumulate.

rationales.A: Ribosomes make enzymes independent of the Golgi complex, and the drug is stated not to affect synthesis.
rationales.B: The Golgi complex modifies and packages proteins; it does not digest them or speed up breakdown of cell components.
rationales.C: Lysosomal enzymes are made at the rough ER; the lysosome receives them and does not make them.
rationales.D: Packaging in the Golgi complex is required to deliver enzymes to lysosomes, so digestion falls and material accumulates.

stem: A biologist examines four cell types for organelles. Cell W secretes large amounts of a protein hormone. Cell X secretes a steroid hormone, which is a lipid. Cell Y contracts and contains many mitochondria. Cell Z stores fat in a large droplet. Protein destined for secretion is made on the rough ER and then processed by the Golgi complex. Which cell would be expected to have the most extensive rough ER and Golgi complex?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Cell X, because lipids such as steroids are made on the rough ER and then secreted in vesicles from the Golgi.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Cell Z, because a large droplet of fat has to be packaged by the Golgi complex before it can be stored.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Cell W, because making and secreting a large amount of protein depends on the rough ER and Golgi complex.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Cell Y, because the many mitochondria in the cell supply the protein that the rough ER and Golgi complex store.

rationales.A: Steroid hormones are lipids made by smooth ER, so Cell X would be expected to have extensive smooth ER, not rough ER.
rationales.B: Stored fat in a droplet is not made or secreted through the rough ER and Golgi pathway, so this cell has little need for them.
rationales.C: A cell that secretes a lot of protein needs many ribosomes on rough ER and extensive Golgi processing and packaging.
rationales.D: Mitochondria supply ATP and do not make protein for the rough ER and Golgi; a contractile cell does not secrete large amounts of protein.

stem: Evidence supporting the endosymbiotic origin of chloroplasts includes: (1) chloroplasts are surrounded by two membranes, with the inner one resembling a bacterial plasma membrane and the outer one resembling the host's membrane; (2) chloroplasts have their own circular DNA; (3) chloroplasts have 70S ribosomes like those of bacteria; (4) chloroplasts divide in a way similar to binary fission. Which single piece of evidence most specifically supports the claim that a prokaryote was taken up by a host cell, rather than just showing prokaryote-like features?

choices.label: A
choices.text: The division like binary fission shows that chloroplasts are fully independent prokaryotes that live inside the plant cell.

choices.label: B
choices.text: The circular DNA shows that chloroplasts can still live outside plant cells in the way that free-living bacteria do.

choices.label: C
choices.text: The 70S ribosomes show that chloroplasts take in whole bacteria from the environment when plant cells divide.

choices.label: D
choices.text: The two membranes, with an inner layer like a bacterial plasma membrane and an outer layer like the host, match a prokaryote taken in inside a host membrane.

rationales.A: Division resembling binary fission shows prokaryote-like reproduction, but chloroplasts rely on the host and are not independent prokaryotes.
rationales.B: Circular DNA shows similarity to prokaryotes; it does not show independence, and chloroplasts depend on their host cells.
rationales.C: Ribosome type shows similarity to bacteria; it does not describe uptake of bacteria.
rationales.D: The double membrane is the structural result expected if a host cell engulfed a prokaryote in a vesicle.

stem: Antibiotic Q blocks protein synthesis on 70S ribosomes of bacteria but does not affect the 80S ribosomes found in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells. Mitochondria contain their own ribosomes. If mitochondria arose from engulfed bacteria, which result is most likely when human cells in culture are treated with antibiotic Q?

choices.label: A
choices.text: All protein synthesis stops, because the same ribosome type makes protein in the cytoplasm and in mitochondria.

choices.label: B
choices.text: No protein synthesis is affected, because mitochondria contain no ribosomes and make no protein of their own.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Protein synthesis inside mitochondria is inhibited, while protein synthesis on cytoplasmic ribosomes continues.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Protein synthesis on cytoplasmic ribosomes is inhibited, while mitochondrial protein synthesis continues without change.

rationales.A: This assumes one ribosome type works in both places. If mitochondria arose from bacteria, their ribosomes resemble bacterial 70S ribosomes and differ from the 80S cytoplasmic ribosomes, so antibiotic Q would not stop all protein synthesis.
rationales.B: Mitochondria are stated to have their own ribosomes and they do make some of their own proteins.
rationales.C: If mitochondrial ribosomes resemble bacterial 70S ribosomes, antibiotic Q blocks them but not the cytoplasmic 80S ribosomes.
rationales.D: This reverses the targets: Q affects 70S ribosomes, the type expected in mitochondria, and spares the cytoplasmic 80S ribosomes.

stem: A transmembrane channel protein forms a pore through the plasma membrane that lets ions pass. Researchers analyze the R groups of its amino acids. Which description of the protein's R groups is most consistent with its location and function?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Only nonpolar R groups throughout the protein, since the protein is embedded in the hydrophobic interior of the membrane.

choices.label: B
choices.text: Polar R groups on the outer surface that contacts the phospholipid tails, and nonpolar R groups lining the interior of the pore.

choices.label: C
choices.text: Only polar R groups throughout the protein, since the pore carries ions that are dissolved in the water.

choices.label: D
choices.text: Nonpolar R groups on the outer surface that contacts the phospholipid tails, and polar R groups lining the interior of the pore.

rationales.A: A pore lined only with nonpolar R groups would not let ions pass; the pore lining must be polar.
rationales.B: This reverses the arrangement: polar groups are unstable beside hydrophobic tails, and nonpolar groups would hinder the passage of ions.
rationales.C: Polar groups on the outer surface would not be stable next to the hydrophobic phospholipid tails.
rationales.D: Nonpolar outer R groups are stable next to hydrophobic tails, while polar R groups lining the pore favor passage of ions and water.

stem: Researchers study Protein Q from broken red blood cell membranes. Washing the membranes with a high-salt solution releases Protein Q, and the phospholipid bilayer stays intact. The amino acids on the surface of Protein Q have mostly polar and charged R groups. Which characterization of Protein Q is best supported by these results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A protein dissolved in the interior of the bilayer, with nonpolar R groups that interact with the surrounding water.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A protein attached to the membrane surface by interactions between its polar R groups and the polar heads of phospholipids or other membrane proteins.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A protein embedded in the bilayer, with nonpolar R groups that touch the hydrophobic tails of the phospholipids.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A protein spanning the bilayer, with polar R groups on the surface that touches the phospholipid tails.

rationales.A: Nonpolar R groups do not interact favorably with water, and this protein was released from the surface rather than from the interior.
rationales.B: Easy removal without dissolving the bilayer and a polar surface indicate a surface-associated protein interacting with polar regions.
rationales.C: An embedded protein with a nonpolar surface would not be released by salt and would require dissolving the bilayer.
rationales.D: Polar R groups are not stable next to hydrophobic tails, and a spanning protein would not be released by salt.

stem: A researcher determines the amino acid sequence of Protein T. Seven separate stretches of about 20 amino acids each have only nonpolar R groups, and the regions between the stretches have mostly polar R groups. Protein T can be removed from membranes only by dissolving the lipid bilayer with a detergent. Which description of Protein T is best supported by these results?

choices.label: A
choices.text: A protein attached to the outside of the membrane, with its nonpolar stretches facing the watery fluid around it.

choices.label: B
choices.text: A protein dissolved in the cytoplasm, with its nonpolar stretches facing outward toward the surrounding water.

choices.label: C
choices.text: A protein with all of its polar regions buried in the center of the bilayer, among the hydrophobic tails.

choices.label: D
choices.text: A protein that crosses the bilayer several times, with its nonpolar stretches in the membrane interior and its polar regions outside the bilayer.

rationales.A: Removal requires dissolving the bilayer, so the protein is not simply attached outside, and nonpolar stretches would not face water.
rationales.B: Nonpolar stretches facing water are unstable, and the need for detergent shows Protein T is part of the bilayer, not dissolved.
rationales.C: Polar regions are not stable among the hydrophobic tails; the nonpolar stretches belong there.
rationales.D: Nonpolar stretches fit among the hydrophobic tails, while polar regions stay in the aqueous environments on either side.
